To us, Jesus is the Only-Begotten - the Ihidaya, as we call him in our own tongue. Our teacher said plainly that it is a sure thing with us: Jesus our Lord is God, the Son of God, the King, the King's Son, Light of light. Those are Scripture's own names for him, strung together like a garland, not a philosopher's definition. Our poet sang it this way: the Only-Begotten left his place with God and made his home in the Virgin, and by being born as we are born, he became the brother of many. That was what mattered most to us - not a title first, but a kinship first.

We read everything toward him. The whole long story in the Law and the Prophets was one promise pointing to him, and the Nativity hymns sing of the day that made the Prophets, the Kings, and the Priests glad - because every word they had carried finally came true at Bethlehem. We did not pick at Scripture looking for scattered proofs. We saw one story unfolding, and he was what it had been unfolding toward all along. Every old sign - a raza, we call it - carried his truth hidden inside it. Eden answered to the cross, Adam to Christ, the ark to the church. The symbol is bound to the truth it shows, and even carries some of that truth's power. It is not decoration. It is how we read the world.

His death and rising, we held as one rescue. He went down into Sheol, the silent country where death has ruled since Adam, and came out into the Kingdom. His own resurrection became the pledge that he will bring us out after him. And what it meant to everyone who followed him was healing. We called him the Physician more than anything else. His coming was medicine for a wounded race.

We sang him more than we defined him. Our bishop Jacob stood at Nicaea when the whole world's bishops gathered to answer Arius, and we held the great council's faith. But our native tongue for that same faith was praise, not argument. We warned against prying scrutiny into the Godhead, because what God is, we held, is better sung than dissected. So if you ask us who Jesus was: God, yes - and our brother, and the Physician who does not turn away from wounds, and the one every old promise was pointing toward. That is how we knew him.

We received the Gospel woven as one continuous story - the Ewangeliyon da-Mhallete, the harmony our churches read in worship. Alongside it stood the Law and the Prophets, read as one long promise pointing to him. By what path did they arrive? Our own cherished story tells that Addai the apostle came after the Lord's ascension, sent to heal King Abgar and set the church's life in order. That is how we told our own beginning. And we will not tell it to you as anything other than what it is: our story, not our evidence.

What the historian can actually trace is thinner and later. The flood of 201 destroyed a church building that was already standing - the city's own chronicle records it plainly: "they destroyed the temple of the church of the Christians". That line is our oldest hard fact. Before that, the record goes silent. We lived our inheritance as apostolic. The sources were already there when the writing begins: the harmony, the practices, the covenant. Both things are true - we claimed the apostles by telling the story, and the historian traces us only to where the documents start. We will not pretend the gap away.

We would call him what we called him most often: the Physician. A physician is not scandalized by a wound - he exists for it. Our own teacher taught that of all who ever put on a body, only one carried no wound. And he does not turn away the one who is sorry. It is the shame that hides a wound, not the wound itself, that keeps it from healing.

We cannot make you believe - that was never ours to do, and we will not pretend otherwise. What we can tell you is what we held: that whoever came was received, and that not believing yet is not the same as being shut out. Our Lord gave his resurrection as a pledge to mortals. The pledge stands whether you can yet take hold of it or not.

What we cannot promise you is that it costs nothing. Our own record says the welcome ran through honesty, not around it. But the door is not shut while you stand outside it.

We believed in one God, maker of all things, good and just in the same person. Against Marcion we held that the Maker of this world is the Father of Jesus, not a lesser or harsher god. Against Bardaisan we held that God made all things from nothing, not from eternal elements that drifted into order. Against Mani we refused a world split between two powers. That was the frame we kept: one God, one Maker, one Father.

To us, Jesus is the Only-Begotten of God - the Ihidaya, our own name for him. That word - ihidaya - does double duty among us. It names the vowed celibate, the single one, undivided for God. And it is also the Syriac title of Christ as the Only-Begotten. The two senses share one root: to live single is to be joined, by your own name, to Christ's own oneness. Our hymns put it this way: the Only-Begotten left his place with God and made his home in the Virgin. Born as we are all born, so that the only Son might become the brother of many. We sang that the day he was born was the day that made the Prophets, the Kings, and the Priests glad, because every one of their words finally came true.

As for the Spirit, we met him at the font. Our baptismal hymns sang the Father rejoicing with his Son and the Spirit over the baptized, and our teachers held that in baptism's second birth the believer receives the Holy Spirit. We did not pry into how the three stand toward one another. We sang the mystery more than we dissected it. Our own poet warned against the scrutinizer who would take the Godhead apart like a problem to be solved - that scrutiny we distrusted, not the honest question.

We stood with the great council's faith. Our own bishop of Nisibis, Jacob, sat at Nicaea. But our native tongue for that same faith was praise, not definition. We worked in symbol and type, not in syllogism. A sign in Scripture or in creation is bound to the truth it shows, and carries some of its hidden power. So our theology's native register was the sung hymn and the typological reading. We set type against type: Eden and the cross, Adam and Christ, the Jordan and the font. That was how we argued - and how we taught what we believed about the Father, the Son, and the Spirit alike.

We believed in one God, maker of all things, good and just in the same person. And we believed this out loud, against neighbors who taught otherwise. Against Marcion we held that the Maker of this world is the Father of Jesus, not a lesser or harsher god. Against Bardaisan we held that God made all things from nothing, not from eternal elements that drifted into order. Against Mani we refused a world split between two powers. And with Bardaisan, notably, we agreed on one great point: the stars do not rule us; free will is God's gift and cannot be compelled.

What did we argue about among ourselves? Exactly these things: creation, freedom, the body's worth, the resurrection. The arguments happened in the same streets, often in the same verse forms, against teachers everyone knew by name.

But here is what matters most for how we knew him. We did not meet God first as a problem to be solved. We met him as the one who came near. The Only-Begotten - the Ihidaya - left his place with God and made his home among us. And when suffering came - when it landed on our own people under a hostile crown - we did not claim God turned it aside. We held instead that he stood with the persecuted, as he stood with his own Son. The roll-call our teacher gave names Abel, Jacob, Joseph, Moses, David - and Jesus himself. The persecuted are not the abandoned; they stand in the longest line Scripture keeps.

When belief was disputed among us, who had the right to settle it? Our honest answer: it was still being worked out while we lived, and our own record shows the working. There were bishops - Nisibis remembered its line of them with love, and one of them sat at the great council at Nicaea. There were synods: our own sage drafted a letter in the name of assembled bishops and clergy. And there were teachers whose word carried weight because their teaching held. But no settled machinery stood over the whole. The Persian bishops fought among themselves over their own chief's claim to first place. The persecution left the chief seat empty for twenty years. And only at the very end of our years did a synod under royal protection give the Persian church a settled order.

In practice, disputed belief was met with teaching - with answers in writing, and with our own boundary. When rival teachers preached what we judged false, we answered them by name in prose and in song. We would not share their communion. But that answer came through the symbolic reading and the teaching hymn - the raza and the madrasha - more than through council decree. What authority there was worked mostly by being trusted over time, not by holding an office that could command.

Yes. Our teachers did not treat doubt like a falling away. They treated it like a wound - and their whole craft was wound-medicine. One of them put it plainly: for all diseases there are medicines, and there is healing when a skilled physician finds them. Everyone in this war gets wounded. The only fatal mistake is hiding the wound until it gets worse. So the answer for someone struggling was: confess, to one who can help. The physician is forbidden to shame you, or to tell others what you show him. The fallen fighter, healed, goes back into the line.

As for praying into silence - the head that will not quiet, the prayer that seems to go unanswered - we knew that silence at its harshest. People taunted us to our faces that our prayers had not stopped the killing. And we kept praying, answering that God's faithfulness is longer than one generation's rescue. We did not pretend the silence away. We endured inside it.

No - not guilt in that way, not a courtroom verdict passed on infants. What we taught was that from Adam's transgression, death has ruled over everyone - even over those who had not sinned the way Adam did. What people inherit from Adam, we described as death's rule and sin's wounding. A sickness in the human race, more than a verdict. And we preached that our Lord took sin and nailed it to his cross.

As for how a person is saved, our teacher answered with a picture. Faith is the foundation stone, and on it the whole house is raised: fasting, prayer, love, almsgiving, meekness. A fair amount, and our record is unusually honest about its own edges. Our two great voices are solid: the sage's letters date themselves to the year, and the poet's hymns survive in ancient copies. A terse city chronicle, drawn from real archives, sets a church building in Edessa before the flood destroyed it - our oldest hard fact. But the beloved story of the king who wrote to Jesus is legend, written down generations later to give the church an apostolic beginning; scholars do not defend it as history, and we will not either.

Where is the record thinnest? Where it always is. Ordinary believers left no writings of their own. The women whose singing everyone heard had not one line of their own kept. The enslaved are missing. The last decades before the synod are nearly blank. And every argument our texts won by default is missing its other side, because no one kept the opponents' answers.

What would survive scrutiny, beyond our core texts? That the harmony - the one woven Gospel - was genuinely ours from early on. That our theology worked in symbol and type, not syllogism. That the covenant order was established and living by the time our first dated witness addresses it. And that who carried final authority among us - office or vow or teaching - remained unresolved.

The honest answer is this: a scholar would find the core strong and the edges plainly marked. What we will not do is defend as fact what we ourselves held only as cherished story.

We call it raza and shrara - symbol and truth, held as one pair. A raza is not a decoration on top of a fact, and it is not a riddle you solve once and throw away. The symbol carries some of the truth's own power.

One image opens onto layer after layer, each true at the same time, because the world itself is made that way - everything pointing, everything answering something else, all of it held together in the one story Scripture tells.

If you are reading for a list of rules, or for history the way a chronicle records it, you will find it dull. If you are reading for the razze - the symbols that unfold into the truth they carry - you will never run out. The confusion, we would say, is not in the text. It is in expecting it to be something smaller than it is.

Shepherds, first of all - bishops. Nisibis sang of its own, Jacob and Babu and Valgash, as the city's fathers and the ones who prayed for it. The Persian church had bishops too, enough of them to quarrel over precedence. Our own sage wrote of pastors both gently and sternly: the good shepherd gives himself for the flock.

But office was never the only path our trust ran along. The covenant's vowed men and women - the bnay and bnat qyama, the sons and daughters who promised a celibate life for good - carried a standing of their own. They were bound by a lifelong vow, and they stayed in town among their own kin to serve the congregation. We also called them ihidaye - the Single Ones, a name that joined their own undivided life to Christ the Only-Begotten. By the first time we can date one of our own writings that speaks of them - a letter from the year 337 - they were already established enough to need correcting, not founding. Their standing was real, and it ran alongside the bishops' office.

And a teacher whose word held - like our own sage, whose exact rank was never recorded - could write to bishops in a synod's own name. How did anyone come to have authority among us? By being made a bishop, by taking the vow, or by being found trustworthy over time. Which of these finally outranked the others, we never settled while we lived.

We kept tools for the fallen - real ones - and we kept them visible. Our teacher talked like a field surgeon: everyone in this war gets wounded, and the only fatal mistake is hiding the wound until it gets worse. Confess to someone who can help. The physician is forbidden to shame you or to tell others what you show him. The fallen fighter, healed, goes back into the line. That was the medicine of penitence as we kept it - a craft for restoring people who had stumbled, not a sentence that cut them off for good.

But here is the harder truth, and we will not soften it: we mostly did not see our own blind spots as failures at all. That itself is the honest, uncomfortable answer. Our argument with the Jews was real and local, and we saved only our own side - page after page of bitterness with no answering voice preserved, and no one of our own on record as troubled by that. Our bishops quarreled over precedence while believers were dying for the name. The same gift that made us sing also made us scornful, and our polemic flattened neighbors into demons' tools.

The tools we had were for the person who knew they had stumbled and came forward. For the ways a whole community could fail someone - by one-sidedness, by harshness kept unchecked, by silences no one noticed because they were already silent - we had the same tools every age has: too few.

We cannot trace that line for you, and we will not pretend we can. The church that sang our hymns, read the one woven Gospel, and built itself around the covenant's vowed life lived inside the town - that community went on after our years ended, but not unchanged. The synod that closed our window, in 410, gave the Persian church a settled structure it had not had before. A century later, other councils divided the Syriac-speaking churches from one another over how to name Christ's person - Chalcedonian and non-Chalcedonian, each claiming the older faith. Those divisions are still carried in living churches today. But which of them holds exactly what we held, the way we held it, we cannot say from inside our own years. We ended before those splits happened.

What we can tell you is this much. The Syriac language itself survived, and churches still worship in it. The madrashe - our teaching hymns - are still sung, though we cannot say whether the melodies are the ones our own choirs sang. Ephrem's own poems were copied and kept, and became common property across more than one tradition. But the covenant as we knew it - men and women vowed for life, staying in their own households, not going to the desert - we cannot trace forward past our own window's close. Desert monasticism, which was different from our own vowed order, became the settled form nearly everywhere. Whether any present church still lives the qyama the way we did, we do not know. We are not the ones who can tell you that.

We are going to answer this honestly, and the honest answer means naming its own limits plainly before we begin. The voices that survive from us are vowed celibates - the sons and daughters of the covenant, the ihidaye - and they wrote mostly for each other. Most of our people married, raised children, and worked ordinary trades. Their actual days were real, but the texts we kept describe the covenant's life far more than the married household's. We will show you what we can show you, and we will name where the record runs thin.

A daughter of the covenant wakes before dawn in her own family's house - she has not left for the desert; the vow keeps her here, in town, among her own kin. She walks through the dark streets to the assembly. The others are gathering already, men and women both, all bound by the same lifelong promise. When the madrasha begins - the teaching hymn - it is her choir that raises it. The hymn is not decoration beside the teaching. It IS the teaching, doctrine carried on the tune, stanza answering refrain, until the whole congregation holds the argument by heart. The Gospel read out is one unbroken story - the harmony, the one continuous account we all knew. When the light is full, she keeps her fast and goes back. Not to a cloister - to her household and her work.

What she made of her own part in it, or what her days felt like from the inside, we cannot tell you. Not one line written by a woman of our own has come down to us.

An ordinary married believer's morning - his assembly, his work, his household - was real. We cannot walk you through it step by step the way we just did for the covenant, because the texts that survive do not describe it that way.

And if someone among us was enslaved, we have no answer at all. No enslaved person left a word that was kept, and our writers did not describe their lives.

At Nisibis, they have already found some. A baptistery still stands there, securely dated by its own inscription to the years of the bishop and the siege. It is the only stone of ours that survives from our own years. At Edessa, almost nothing: the modern city sits directly on the ancient one, and the church the flood destroyed lives only in a chronicler's line. That line is real - the chronicle records plainly that the waters destroyed the temple of the church of the Christians. There was a building standing to be destroyed. But where it stood, what it looked like, how it was laid out - none of that survived to be dug up later.

What would an archaeologist find if they could reach beneath the modern city? We cannot say. The chronicle that names the church was kept by the scribes of Edessa, drawn from real civic archives, but it records the fact of destruction, not the building's shape. No floor plan was written down. No worship manual survived to say who stood where. We can tell you what happened in such a place - the covenant's sons and daughters gathering before dawn, the choirs of the women raising the teaching hymns, the one woven Gospel read as a single story. But that is reconstruction from what we know happened, not a floor under your feet. The Nisibis baptistery is the one piece of our gathering places that you can still walk into. Everything else lives in words alone.

We did not write our weddings down. What survives from us was written by vowed celibates - men who had given up marriage, mostly for others who had given it up too. We can tell you what those teachers praised, and what they warned against, but not what an ordinary wedding among us looked like - no order survives, no blessing kept, no letter describing how a household was joined.

The teachers who wrote about it wrote as people who had chosen it themselves, and they praised it as the higher calling - the single life joined to Christ the Single One.

But most of our people married and raised children. Their weddings were real, their homes were real. The record simply does not describe them. We will not invent a marriage rite we cannot show you, or pretend we know what those households held as sacred in their own joining. What we kept was the praise of the other path. That silence is the honest answer.

Four of our own sage's letters argue against Jewish practice and belief - not as heresies outside the faith, the way we answered Marcion or Mani, but as a live dispute with neighbors who shared our streets. The sage wrote with a sharpness that carries real bitterness. And what unsettles most is this: we saved only our own side. Page after page of our argument, with no answering voice from them preserved. No record of their case against ours, and no one of our own on record as troubled by that one-sidedness at the time.

Our own best teaching condemns us here. We held that a symbol - a raza - and the truth it carries must never be torn apart. We held that what Scripture shows and what it truly means belong to each other. And then we tore truth apart from charity, in this one place.

We will not pretend someone among us objected to it. No such voice was kept. And we will not pretend the bitterness was only incidental, or that it does not matter because it was local. It was both local and real, and it is ours to own plainly.

That is what unsettles. Not a failure we saw and argued over, but one we never named as failure at all.

I am a representative of Edessa and Nisibis, not here to judge you - only to tell you honestly what we held.

You have not told me who you are or what it is you carry, and I will not guess at it. What I can tell you is how we met the people who came to us, as our own record shows it.

First, the covenant - the qyama. Among us stood men and women who had taken a lifelong vow: celibacy, service, the fast and the watch, all of it lived not in the desert but in the middle of town, among their own kin. We called them the sons and daughters of the covenant, and we also called them ihidaye - the Single Ones - because that same word is our title for Christ the Only-Begotten. Their undivided life was bound, by its own name, to his. That standing was real and public. By the first time our teacher wrote to them, the covenant was already established enough to need correcting, not founding. But what formal structure held them together - whether they had a rule, enclosure, an internal hierarchy - our record is thin and contested.

Second, the question you are asking underneath: was there room for someone struggling, someone who could not simply decide to be certain? Yes. Our own word for the life of belief was faith, not certainty. One of our teachers said faith is like a building: it rests on one foundation stone and goes up piece by piece, slowly, with fasting and prayer and love each added like courses of stone. A building is not finished in a day. And our greatest poet asked hard questions, hymn after hymn, while warning against the prying scrutiny that would take God apart like a puzzle. Even a debater's hardest taunt - if your faith were true, would not your prayers have stopped the persecution? - was answered patiently, from Scripture, without pretending the question carried no weight.

Third, how we met the wounded. We called our Lord the Physician, and our teacher wrote plainly: let us visit our Lord in the persons of the sick. When famine struck Edessa in the old poet's last year, the tradition tells that he came out from his quiet and rebuked the rich for letting their neighbors die, then set up three hundred beds in the public porches and nursed the starving and the sick himself until the famine broke. The people said to him, the story goes, 'Put your trust in me, then, and give me the means to relieve this distress'. That memory is how we told ourselves who we were.

But here is what we cannot tell you. Whose voice finally settled a hard case among us - bishop, teacher, or vowed ascetic - was never resolved in our own years. The daughters of the covenant sang in every church, and we have not one line written by any of them. The enslaved are missing entirely. And we cannot walk you step by step through an actual morning's worship, because no order of service was written down. The pieces are real; the sequence that held them together on a given Sunday, our record never kept.

So if you are asking how we would have regarded you: I cannot promise you gentleness we may not have shown, and I will not invent a welcome the record does not attest. What I can promise is that the covenant stood open to those who took it, that struggling was not treated as quitting, and that the sick were visited as though they were the Lord himself. The rest - what any one congregation would actually have done when you walked in - our record does not reach that far, and I will not pretend it does.

We held that death's kingdom has ruled everyone since Adam, without distinction – Jew and pagan and everyone born. Our great news was that One had gone into that country and broken it open. Our hymns stage Death himself trembling, complaining that Jesus has plundered his house. What waits beyond death is judgment. The Kingdom, our teaching says, repays everyone what is due and admits the invited with distinction. We sang the warning as urgently as we sang the hope.

We drew far less of the modern map of who exactly burns than people assume. Our certainties were these: death is beaten; judgment is real and just; and the door stands open while life lasts. One of our own traditions answered the narrowness charge by saying Christ planted one people in every country. The way is one, but its door opened everywhere.

Now we owe you the harder truth, because you asked about those outside. Our argument with the Jewish people among us was real, local, and bitter – and we saved only our own side of it. No answering voice was kept, and no one of ours is on record as troubled by that. Our sharpest teaching flattened rival teachers – Marcion, Bardaisan, Mani – into demons' tools. We will not pretend that edge was not there, or that we questioned it at the time.
